name: Active Directory & Exchange
coverAlt: Green Ethernet patch cables connected to a bank of network ports.
summary: Built a Windows domain and verified that users could resolve names and send mail across the lab.
purpose: A working mailbox depends on several services agreeing about a user and a host. I built an isolated Windows environment to follow that chain from the directory to mail delivery.
steps: Build the directory
I created user accounts and organizational units in Active Directory Domain Services, then configured Group Policy for the lab.
Check name resolution
I set up DNS, validated the records, and troubleshot domain communication before moving on to Exchange.
Follow a message
I installed and configured Exchange Server 2019, set up POP and IMAP access, and checked mail flow end to end.
result: The lab domain resolved the required names and Exchange delivered test mail. Checking DNS separately gave me a way to narrow down a mail problem before changing Exchange settings.
takeaway: Test the dependencies first. A mail-flow issue can start with an incorrect DNS record.

name: Custom PC builds
coverAlt: Copper light on a graphics card fan, heatsink fins, and the inside of a desktop PC.
summary: Selected compatible parts, assembled complete desktops, and tested each system before resale.
purpose: Building for someone else means taking responsibility for the whole machine. I carried custom desktop systems from the parts list through assembly, troubleshooting, testing, and sale.
steps: Select compatible parts
I selected components for each build and checked that they would work together as a complete system.
Assemble and troubleshoot
I assembled each desktop and worked through hardware issues that came up during the build.
Test before handoff
I tested completed systems before offering them for resale.
result: I sold completed, tested desktops that I had built myself. The project gave me practice making component decisions and troubleshooting the finished machine.
takeaway: A parts list is only the start. The finished system is what the next owner has to rely on.

name: Virtualization home lab
coverAlt: A stack of compact metal servers lit in cool blue.
summary: Built an isolated ESXi environment for virtual machines, containers, and network testing.
purpose: I wanted a place to test how servers and network policies behave without disturbing everyday systems. VMware ESXi gave me a separate environment for running those experiments.
steps: Build the test environment
I set up VMware ESXi and provisioned virtual machines and container workloads for isolated testing.
Control traffic
I configured load balancing and firewall rules so I could test how traffic moved through the environment.
Inspect the logs
I reviewed firewall logs alongside the configured rules to see what traffic the lab actually allowed.
result: The lab provided a repeatable environment for testing network changes and observing their effects in logs.
takeaway: A firewall rule describes an intention. Its logs help show what actually happened.

name: Veeam backup solution design
summary: Designed a backup and recovery plan for a Proxmox lab, including storage, retention, and exclusions.
purpose: A Proxmox home lab needed a plan for what to protect, how long to keep it, and how to recover it. I used those questions to define the backup design.
steps: Define coverage
I outlined the recovery policies and identified exclusions as part of the backup scope.
Plan storage
I planned mirrored SSDs for boot storage and a ZFS storage target for backups.
Specify retention
I set out how backup copies should be retained and linked those choices to the lab’s recovery needs.
result: The design documented a proposed storage layout and policies for retention, exclusions, and recovery. My separate Veeam deployment lab covers the hands-on backup and restore work.
takeaway: Writing down exclusions is part of a recovery plan. They show exactly what the plan covers.

name: Local LLM deployment
summary: Ran LLaMA and Falcon offline and tuned context size and resource allocation for local hardware.
purpose: I wanted to run language models without sending prompts to an external service. The project was as much about fitting the workload to local hardware as it was about starting a model.
steps: Deploy locally
I set up LLaMA and Falcon in an offline environment and used Open WebUI as a local interface.
Work within resource limits
I adjusted context size, resource allocation, and quantization settings to fit the available hardware.
Compare behaviour
I compared how the models responded as I varied those settings and the amount of context supplied.
result: Both model families ran locally. Tuning the configuration gave me practical experience with the trade-off between context length, memory use, and responsiveness.
takeaway: The best context setting depends on both the prompt and the hardware available to serve it.

name: Loaner laptop refurbishment
summary: Reclaimed compatible RAM and storage, installed Windows, and checked loaner laptops for deployment.
purpose: Retired hardware could still serve students if the replacement parts were compatible and the finished laptops were dependable. I helped prepare loaner devices for end users at Algonquin College.
steps: Match the parts
I selected compatible reclaimed SO-DIMM RAM and NVMe storage for the loaner laptops.
Restore the machines
I installed the hardware and a fresh copy of Windows to prepare each device for use.
Validate the finished device
I checked component compatibility, system health, and operation after both the upgrades and the Windows installation.
result: The refurbished laptops were prepared and checked for end users. Reusing working components turned retired hardware into useful loaner equipment.
takeaway: The repair is complete when the laptop works as a whole after imaging.

name: Kismet wireless sensor
summary: Used wireless telemetry to document access points, channels, signal behaviour, and client associations in a lab.
purpose: A client’s connected status answers only one question about a wireless network. I built a lab sensor to see how channel use, signal behaviour, and associations fit together.
steps: Set up the sensor
I configured a Kismet sensor for monitoring wireless activity in the lab.
Read the radio context
I examined access points, client associations, channels, and signal behaviour together.
Document the observations
I translated the captured telemetry into structured findings and investigation notes.
result: The sensor gave me a view of 802.11 activity that I could describe in technical reports, including how observations related to channel and signal context.
takeaway: A device identifier alone gives an incomplete picture of what is happening on a channel.

name: Self-hosted Jellyfin server
summary: Hosted a media service on a Linux VM, configured HTTPS through Apache, and wrote an administrator guide.
purpose: I wanted to run a media service I could maintain myself, including the route users took to reach it and the information needed to administer it later.
steps: Host the application
I installed Jellyfin on a Linux virtual machine.
Configure the front end
I placed Apache in front of the service as a reverse proxy and configured HTTPS access.
Document administration
I wrote an administrator guide covering the service and its role-based administration.
result: The media service was reachable over HTTPS and had a written administration guide for ongoing maintenance.
takeaway: Knowing where the proxy ends and the application begins makes their logs easier to interpret.

name: Veeam backup & restore lab
summary: Configured backup repositories and agents, then exercised backup and restore procedures in a lab.
purpose: I wanted to verify the recovery path for systems and endpoints, including the repositories and policies behind a backup job.
steps: Set up repositories
I configured Veeam Backup & Replication with multiple repositories and retention policies.
Connect endpoints
I implemented agents to include endpoints in the backup workflow.
Exercise recovery
I tested backup and restore procedures to check how the configured recovery path behaved.
result: The lab included tested backup and restore procedures. I later applied that experience to a separate backup design for a Proxmox home lab.
takeaway: A completed backup job and a successful restore answer different operational questions.
